beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about building a tool server an AI agent can discover on its own. Today we are going to learn the three calls that make that work, by writing one small enough to read in full. The surprising part is how little there is to it.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the topic

props.command: What does a server have to do before an agent can find and use its tools?
output: Three calls: list what exists, describe one, run one.
The client is told nothing in advance. It asks.
Everything else a real server adds is transport, not concept.

beats.narration_text: A tool server does three things and the order matters. It lists what it offers, because the client arrives knowing nothing. It describes any one of those in full, so the client can decide. And it runs one when asked. Discovery, description, invocation.

layers.title: List what exists
layers.sub: the client arrives knowing nothing and asks

layers.title: Run it
layers.sub: and refuse anything that was not on the list

props.caption: Everything else a production server adds is transport, not concept.

beats.narration_text: So here is a client connecting to a server it was told nothing about. It asks what exists and gets back two tools it had never heard of, each with a one-line summary. Nobody configured that list. The server generated it from the functions it had registered.

show.event: the first discovered tool writes on

props.artifactTitle: server.py — the client asks what exists
artifactLines: column_names   List the column headers of a CSV file, in order.
row_count      Count data rows in a CSV file, excluding the header.
props.sparkLine: It had never heard of these.

beats.act: ACT 2 — WHERE THE DESCRIPTION COMES FROM
beats.narration_text: Which raises the obvious question. If nobody wrote that list, where did the descriptions come from? And the answer is the thing I would most want a beginner to take away from this.

props.title: Where Did the Words Come From?
props.body: Nobody wrote the tool list by hand. So where did the descriptions the agent reads actually come from?

beats.act: ACT 2 — WHERE THE DESCRIPTION COMES FROM
beats.narration_text: From the docstring. The server reads the function's own documentation and the signature, and that becomes the contract the agent sees. Which means the comment you wrote for the next developer is now the thing a machine uses to decide whether to call your code.

show.event: the registry lookup and refusal write on
getdoc lands as the voice says 'docstring'

props.title: server.py — describe()

beats.act: ACT 2 — WHERE THE DESCRIPTION COMES FROM
beats.narration_text: And in full it looks like this. The name from the function. The description straight from the docstring, including the line telling the agent what not to use it for. And a parameter schema built from the signature. Three things, none of them written twice.

show.event: the description lands, docstring and all
the do-not line holds in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: Everything the agent will ever see
artifactLines: "description": "Count data rows in a CSV file, excluding
the header. Use this when you need the size
of a file. Do NOT use it to read values.",

beats.narration_text: Then the test that matters more than any successful call. Ask the server for a tool that does not exist and it refuses by name. It does not guess, does not find something similar, and does not invent a result. The list it published is the complete set of things it will do.

props.sparkLine: The list is the whole set.
items: A real tool runs and returns
An unknown tool is refused by name
props.caption: Discovery is only meaningful if the published list is exhaustive.

beats.narration_text: Both outcomes, side by side. A known tool runs and returns three. An unknown one comes back as a refusal naming exactly what was asked for. That second line is what makes the first one trustworthy, because a server that improvises when it does not recognise something cannot be reasoned about at all.

show.event: the successful call writes on and returns 3
the unknown call lands as a named refusal, in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: The refusal is what makes the success meaningful

beats.narration_text: One more thing the server enforces, and it is a small cruelty I would recommend. A function with no docstring cannot be registered at all. Not a warning, not an empty description. If you cannot say what it does, the agent has no way to decide whether to call it, so it does not get offered.

show.event: the two branches light in order
arc completes toward the published list

props.destTitle: contains only tools that can describe themselves
props.arcCaption: an undescribed tool is worse than a missing one

beats.narration_text: What this file is not is a production server. There is no transport, no session, no authentication, and no error semantics beyond raising. Those are real work. But none of them change the three calls, and the three calls are the part worth understanding first.

props.title: This Is Not a Production Server
props.body: No transport, no session, no authentication, no error semantics. All real work — and none of it changes the three calls underneath.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A tool server does three things: it lists what it offers to a client that was told nothing, it describes any one of them in full, and it runs one when asked. The descriptions are not configured anywhere; they are read from the functions' own docstrings, which means the comment you wrote for the next developer is what a machine now uses to decide whether to call your code. A function without a docstring is refused at registration rather than offered with an empty description. And an unknown tool comes back as a refusal naming what was asked, because a server that improvises cannot be reasoned about. Transport, sessions and authentication are real work that none of this replaces.

show.event: the docstring-as-contract line holds in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: Three calls, and a docstring that became a contract

No docstring means no registration. An undescribed tool is worse than a missing one.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take three functions from my codebase and write the tool contract an agent would receive for each: the name, the description from the docstring, and the parameter schema. Then tell me which of the three an agent could not safely choose between, and why. Run it on code you already have. The pair it confuses will be the pair whose docstrings you wrote in the same five minutes.

props.command: Take three functions from my codebase and write the tool contract an agent would receive for each: name, description from the docstring, parameter schema. Then tell me which of the three an agent could not safely choose between, and why.
output: The pair it confuses is usually the pair whose docstrings you wrote together.
If a docstring was written for a human skimming, it will not survive being a contract.

beats.narration_text: That was building a tool server. Next time, what goes wrong once an agent can both use tools and read text it did not write. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
